[SPEAKER_00]
Hello and welcome to the Series B podcast. I'm your host, Greg Pokeriki. Your guest today is Rohit Gupta, Managing Director of Future Communities Capital, an early stage venture capital firm in the Bay Area. Rohit has been a 43 North Judge and is now invested in several Buffalo startups, including Helix Intel. He's bullish on Buffalo's innovation economy, and you'll see why in our conversation here.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thank you. Excited to sort of chat about all things startups and Buffalo and everything in between.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. So for the uninitiated, tell us about Future Communities Capital.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, Future Committee is capital. We're an early stage VC fund. So most of our activity is pre-seed and seed, a little bit of series A, but it's not really core for us. And we focus on legacy industries. So you think about like big, really tough, slow to change, slow to adopt change, which right now is kind of like everybody. If you believe in sort of the future of AI, like what isn't legacy at this point? Yeah, but a few key areas for us, we do a lot of healthcare, some supply chain, some climate, almost a general is fun, but there's a few areas that we just kind of don't touch.

[SPEAKER_00]
So I know part of the... the the core or the ethos is to like find investments outside of the valley right and that's how you got connected into buffalo you've made a couple different investments here in in helix i know finta agnami so really like i want to start with what did you see in buffalo specifically and then get into those companies maybe but like what piqued your interest about buffalo what got you investing here

[SPEAKER_01]
So a long time ago, I was a judge for 43 North and they got me out there. Randomly, I'm pretty sure they found me off a pitch book and... Colleen was out here. And Zoom. Even more random, we were both in LA on the same day. And so I'm up here in the Bay Area and we were both in LA. She's like, do you want to meet? I said, sure. And I didn't really understand why or what was going on or what the program was. We met, we got coffee and she was kind of telling me about Buffalo. It's this emerging sort of ecosystem. And I said, yeah, I'm in, you know, I want to check it out. Like I spent a couple of years in upstate New York, so a little bit familiar, you know, definitely spent a few weekends in Buffalo. I knew the area. I kind of knew that there was a lot of latent sort of like wealth, a lot of like a history of innovation and entrepreneurial vision. And it was an opportunity to kind of come out and learn more about what was happening there and did that for a few years. And by the end of sort of my judging experience there, like I had friends in Buffalo, like I, you know, like text people like, hey, I'm coming to town. We got to meet up. I was coming outside of 43 as well. Yeah. And now I, you know, I genuinely have reasons to go to Buffalo. So it's, it's been a wild ride. Yeah. Still�, it's up.

[SPEAKER_00]
And then how did you get plugged into some of those specific companies and what maybe drew you to investing in them?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, again, there's a single person. It was Pete Borkowski. So, I mean, everybody knows Pete. Everybody loves Pete. For the minutes they should be remembered.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yep.

[SPEAKER_01]
he sent me an email one day like hey I'm leaving 43 and I got this startup would love to talk to you about it and somehow it just sort of sat in my inbox for like a month and finally I was like dude I'm so sorry I missed this and we got on the phone and you know with him and John and what they're building at Helix and so I jumped joined Helix and John you know like founderline intros are the way to do business right he's like hey I got this friend he's at this company it's in sleep and you know like he's very respectful not like I need you to meet this guy and I said yeah I get it let me I would love to meet Agnomi I did some homework around sleep apnea and yeah did that deal too and from there it's just sort of been Yeah.

[SPEAKER_00]
Pretty good clip. So you talked about, you know, I get introduced to those two founders. It was like an individual each time beyond just those two companies. broadly as you think about investing and looking at evaluating founders. Like, what do you look for in a founder? How do you... kind of decide which which founder to to jockey how do you start to evaluate them through those early conversations

[SPEAKER_01]
That's sort of the heart of the game, right? And I think it depends where an investor is sort of putting their money. Because if I'm a late-stage investor, obviously the people matter, the founders matter. Hopefully they're still there, there's a different CEO, whoever's running it. But really the company's set. right product they're already in market hopefully they're They're generating returns. It's a going concern. Company culture is there. It's like trying to turn an aircraft carrier at that point, right? But at early stage, it is so dependent on people. Because if, let's say you came to me, oh, I got this thing I want to do. Between that and launching, and then sort of like taking off and sort of... reaching orbit or something it's going to pivot five ten times right and so if i hedge my entire bet on this product this idea and that's what i love and that's what i want to back it just doesn't work right It has to be about the people. And I'm probably an outlier in the sense that I will never invest in somebody I do not like. I have to personally like somebody and believe in them in order for me to say I want to do this. I mean, my life is short. I guess I'm privileged in a way to say I don't want to do business with people that I do not like or I do not like the way they do business or treat people.

[SPEAKER_00]
I've heard about you talk about in previous interviews or podcasts, like how much the people matter to building an ecosystem, especially in these somewhat more nascent cities outside of the valley. Can you talk to us a little bit about that and maybe what you saw in Buffalo early on and the idea of like people kind of helping each other out and laying the foundation for an ecosystem that we could build upon?

[SPEAKER_01]
But that I think runs through an entirety of venture, no matter where you work. And I think the ecosystems that sort of really push that are ones that do well, right? And you come out here and people happily make intros. They don't think twice. And a lot of that is... You know, like Brad Fell has that ethos of give first, you know, give, help people without asking or thinking what's in it for me, just help people. But I think a lot of it is also just saying that it's not a zero sum game. Right. And I honestly believe it's it's almost accretive. Right. Like when I help people, it's going to come back to me. You know, I have no problem helping other people raise money because I don't feel that the pool is going to dwindle by helping somebody else raise money. You know, and I think the best founders really push that. And I will say that, you know. John DeWald, fantastic founder. Dude's awesome, right? And by him bringing Agnomi to me, like I have even more respect for him. There's something very real about saying like, John can recognize talent. John can recognize other founders that are winners. And then like, what does that mean for his own team that he's saying like, oh yeah, sure, I get it. I know who I'm investing in, you know, in terms of people, in terms of capital, in terms of whatever, product.

[SPEAKER_00]
I think Buffalo probably specifically or maybe uniquely, like we are the, you know, the city of good neighbors, like the idea of that, like easy intro, like zero hesitation. I think we have strengths in that area. And that's probably some of what you identified that encouraged you to. want to invest here and keep coming back and, you know, make friends here in Buffalo. I'm curious where you see opportunities where Buffalo could mature beyond that. You've talked about the ways in which those relationships help build the foundation of an ecosystem. What advice would you have to Buffalo for the next five years to really continue to grow and accelerate?

[SPEAKER_01]
I probably pull on two threads. One is that it's easier than ever by like an order or two of magnitude to launch something. Right. I was talking with one of my investors yesterday and he said, now's the golden age of entrepreneurship. because of, and specifically Claude Code, anybody can build anything. And I think Buffalo really has an entrepreneurial streak going back like a hundred years, a hundred plus years, 150 years, maybe. right it's sort of there and it comes out and fits and spurs but like I think you enabled that sort of thinking and say, dude, you have an idea. Let's go build it. Let's go try it. You know, it doesn't have to be some like. six months to build an MVP or no our MVP is done this week we're gonna go and try and sell this thing and like a lot of it's saying I'm gonna solve my problem first and then once I solve my problem I know who the customers are. Right? So that's one thing. Take more swings, right? Like the risk. The risk for me, if I'm a founder, the risk for me has gone down dramatically, right? Because it's not like, oh, I need to spend, I need to quit my job and spend two years. And then maybe at the other end of it, I can go get something. you know now it's like dude we're gonna try this out now and if it works it works and if it doesn't we're going to iterate again and again and again and we're just going to get something that's really interesting the other thread is really about capital i mean i think one of the reasons the bay area wins is because there are people to make introductions to Right. And I mean, to the point where it's absurd, the number of funds out here, we almost take it for granted. You go to a coffee shop in San Francisco, there's going to be a VC in there, right? And it's just, there's so many avenues for raising capital here that the ecosystem kind of flows a little bit more easily, right? I mean, my advice to founders is come out here, spend a few weeks, spend a month, spend whatever, and just line up a ton of meetings. You know, try and raise some money out here. and just see how different it is and you know. Like the ecosystem partners, the capital partners in Western New York are great, you know, everyone, but everyone talks to them. And once you sort of like, if I'm a founder, once I've sort of like gone through that whole Rolodex, I have to go outside anyways. It's not possible to sort of raise forever capital. in western new york at some point i need to leave and i feel like the earlier you can diversify your capital stack the better you're going to be in the long term

[SPEAKER_00]
So for those VCs that you're talking about that are kind of lining up in coffee shops out in California, like what do you think that they miss about Buffalo? What do they maybe underestimate about a city like Buffalo or maybe other kind of tertiary, like second tier cities?

[SPEAKER_01]
I was born in San Francisco. Right. And at some point... I looked around and I realized that almost everyone in this game... in the valley is not from the valley, the valley being the entire Bay Area. They're just they're not from here. And so I kind of had this kind of light bulb, lightning, whatever moment where I said, you know, if I can find. founders before they moved to San Francisco all win. And so that really led to this search of What are some locations, what are geographies that are rich in talent, whether it's technical talent, whatever, business talent, you know, idea, whatever, whatever, you know, but really underdeveloped. And I think for me, Buffalo is, I mean, it's probably my second biggest location after like L.A., you know. And so we just... It's... It's got universities, right? So a lot of smart people come out of schools. And it's like, well, what do you do with these smart people? Because they're young, they're ambitious. Do we let them... sort of is there a brain drain or can we sort of keep them in buffalo and i you know i made the point before i think last i was in buffalo and i was Thank you. Thank you. Go ahead, mate. giving a talk about i made the point that you shouldn't have to blow up your life to build a startup because a lot of us are you know you have some experience you have a family you have a partner you have kids you have all this sort of stuff and you shouldn't have to throw all that away and say i'm going to go move to the west coast 3 000 miles away just to pursue this thing if you want to that's great by all means the weather's better You should do it. But if you don't want to, or you can't or whatever, that shouldn't exclude somebody from pursuing their dreams. And I think that like, there are just a lot of founders who are not going to make that move and saying like, hey, I will support you where you are. You know, I'm coming to you. I think that's important to founders. And I think that unlocks a whole lot of opportunities to deploy funds that otherwise I'd be sitting on the sidelines and just saying like, well... I'll talk to you when you move here. You know, I've definitely had fun say like, well, you know like friends who pitch a fund like they want me to move to sf

[SPEAKER_00]
You know, what do you do with that? Right. What's another kind of second tier market that you think is doing a really good job? I think sometimes we get caught in this cycle of looking at like. Boston, New York City, San Francisco, that's not the most realistic or attainable goal for a city like Buffalo. What's a city that you think is doing well that, you know, we could actually like aspire to be? Thank you. and take some real concrete learnings from.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, well, so there's almost two things that are happening, right? There's a lot of cities that sort of in and of themselves have access to capital or talent or something. And it's just kind of organically happening, right? So you could probably put Miami in that bucket because there's capital in Miami. And I think there's tax laws or something that make it easier to want to do these things there. Los Angeles as well. They probably don't want to be called a second tier city. But I think a lot of folks would just say, you just don't have whatever the depth that the Bay Area does. Again, they have capital. They have a lot of talent. You know, I went to school in L.A. and I'm very bullish on USC forever. Fine on. But beyond that, I don't see a lot of cities that intentionally try and build this, right? So in the former category, they're just sort of the ingredients to make a good ecosystem. But to sort of take the next step and say, well, we're going to really push this hard and we want to build this as part of our civic infrastructure. Thank you. right I think, you know, Canada, they make it pretty easy to... to get funding up there through the provinces you know like i've had a couple startups go through the province of nova scotia which honestly like i think a lot of californians couldn't find on a map you know like it's so far east but uh they'll they they want you to move up there and they have phd level talent that you know they will send your way they have industry that they will send your way and like I'd say that's kind of similar to Buffalo, right? You have world-class universities. You have industry there, right? And so you start saying, well, we're going to connect the dots. And then you throw in a program like 43 saying, we're going to financially incentivize companies to come here. And then you start saying like, well, there's a bunch of funds. There's all this other players in the ecosystem. You know, like Jack Greco is a beast. You start getting a couple of guys like him. They come in off the sidelines and say, well, we're going to build this ourselves. The same mindset that a founder has is what, you know, probably makes Jack wake up in the morning and do what he does. So there's a little bit of intentionality there. And then there's a little bit of sort of just having the right ingredients.

[SPEAKER_00]
He touched on some of the ingredients that Buffalo maybe innately has, like the town ecosystem, the universities. University. especially like the existing industries i know like your fund specifically you know targets like legacy industries to invest in and i think it probably is counterintuitive to like the at least maybe the the trope of like startup culture of chase the shiny thing you know what what attracted you to kind of that lane like why do you why does that make you excited to invest and what ways has that like some of the success that you've seen guided that principle

[SPEAKER_01]
Legacy industries, it's sort of a flip way of saying there's opportunity, right? Because you have a giant industry that for whatever reason has not innovated or changed, right? And so I don't think that startups necessarily have to go zero to one every single time. This isn't about creating, you know, the next whatever. It's about saying, here's a process, here's an industry, here's something that we can, you know, improve within the same framework. Dr. Rifkin, founder of Agnomi, been a sleep doctor for 20 something years. And he was early, super early as a neurologist to say, I'm going to focus on sleep. And he said, I'm going to... go brick and mortar because that's what everybody did. And then eventually said, I'm not serving enough people. There are way more people with sleep problems than I can ever. ever serviced through brick and mortar very mission driven and i mean that's i love mission driven companies And he said, I'm going to do this. You know, to the point of saying, he has this entire book of business as a brick and mortar operation. I'm okay with cannibalizing that because it's going to improve patient outcomes. So telehealth versus sleep apnea. If he wasn't the first, he's still one of the only clinically proven. sleep companies out there, sleep startups. Because so many of them are like, we'll give you a relaxation thing or, you know, like try this mattress or this, you know, audio, whatever. I'm not saying those aren't useful. I think a lot of people do have non-clinical sleep, you know, improvements they can make. But for that dude to just jump like that, you know, if that's your talent, that is your entrepreneurial vision, that is, you know, access to capital.

[SPEAKER_00]
What's a maybe legacy industry that's on your mind that you think might be ripe for disruption or maybe that you're not involved in but would like to get involved in?

[SPEAKER_01]
I think there's opportunity in places that are just... Like a lot of opportunities, obvious. right i think right now because we're probably going to face some shortages across the board because of what's happening in iran you know how does that change things on sort of the near term but also the long term because there's there's an opportunity now to sort of affect change that just doesn't get undone right and so specifically like one example that we've been thinking a lot about is electrification if oil really starts to spike in california we're already over six and i've seen seven dollars a gallon in a couple places what does that do and how does that sort of change our thinking on electric vehicles or grid infrastructure or just charging it's already hard enough for a lot of people to charge an ev and then you're like you know? if you sort of take the number of EVs, double it, triplet, quadruple it, where are these people going to charge? And so it's sort of thinking and like playing out, well, this is going to happen and what are the secondary tertiary quaternary effects of that that become really interesting to us.

[SPEAKER_00]
When I think the clean energy transfer space is probably where Buffalo's seen some of the most success, maybe a little bit more on like the. kind of intersection of like tech and manufacturing but it's been a sweet spot for a city like ours kind of changing like you know the rust belt to the green belt type of thing

[SPEAKER_01]
Totally. I mean, there's so much. It's interesting because people try and portray climate as like this doom and gloom thing. But if you look at it from an opportunity standpoint, decarbonization, there's so much money in it, right? Or trying to mitigate the effects of climate change. Like we've been looking a lot at cloud seeding, right? And if you don't know cloud seeding. or your viewers who anyone doesn't know, it's the ability to sort of coax rain out of the sky. you know. And it's one of those things where it's already happening. Part of our deep dive was sort of digging into cloud seeding. You might think that like this is a little far-fetched, but it's already happening in most of the West. And it's definitely happening in California. And so what does that mean to say like, well, the effect of not doing this, like, I don't know if you're a skier, but this year's ski season was cut short, right? California ski resorts have been closing for weeks now. I think Colorado, Utah, some of the worst snowpack they've ever seen. These are all direct effects of climate. Or if you, let's say you don't even believe in climate change. Okay, don't believe in it. do you want to ski You can't say, well, the ski season's shorter, but it's not, right? Like, it's very clearly it's shorter. Historically, it's been getting shorter. And if I can make it snow, what does that mean to people who want to ski? What does that mean to snow pad? What does that mean to just, you know, precipitation in general?

[SPEAKER_00]
I think this parlays pretty well into the last thing I wanted to touch on with you, which is just AI. And you touched on that earlier. You mentioned the ways in which it can speed up the velocity of founding a company, right, and cutting down. Uh-huh. just the amount of time that it takes and maybe even burden that it puts on founders. I'm curious, like in that landscape where it's easier for maybe anybody to do this or start a company, like right earlier, you talked about the value of talent in the individual. How do you sort out like what's a what's a real opportunity in kind of this fast changing landscape, which versus something that that feels kind of cobbled together or maybe, you know, too quick, not as thought out?

[SPEAKER_01]
I'm not sure that that's the actual divide anymore. Right. Because if you can take something that's not as thought out, build it in a weekend launch and get immediate feedback, then that loop becomes so short that the founder figures out real quick, whether there's something there or not. So are we necessarily investing in a bad idea? No, I think it ends up we're investing in this person's vision or their, what they want to, I guess, riff on, you know, in a sense. But the larger context here is that what is it that makes founders successful? It's not product per se. Right. Because, and I mean, I've seen this too, where team spends time building something very thoughtfully comes out the product. That's interesting launches it. And then anybody can copy it within days. Right now, does that copycat have legs? Probably initially, but it becomes, comes down to like, what were they thinking? Right. If it's just, I'm going to copy this, how are they going to improve that product down the line? What does V2 look like? You know? So the first mode is just sort of like vision, taste, design, aesthetics, UI, all that sort of, you can bundle all that together. And then your second mode becomes sort of distribution. Right. Because we kind of look for kind of your earlier question as well, the kind of end of one founder, right? The founder says, I'm the only person who can solve this problem and I'm going to go do it. So one of my favorite companies, a company out of LA is founder, Amantha. She was, she worked in pharmacies for like 20 years, non-technical founder, brilliant person, non-technical. Right. And she said, the problem that I want to solve is independent pharmacies waste a lot of product because they don't really have inventory management. Crazy to believe, but they buy drugs and they just sit on the shelf. And if nobody buys it. They just expire. Insane to think about, right? But that's the way the industry goes. And she said, I'm going to solve this problem because I'm going to enable pharmacy A to sell to pharmacy B. Purely inventory management. and APIs, right? Internally we can... We know what's on the shelf. And then externally, we can offer that to sell to other pharmacies. Her distribution becomes her moat, you know, because let's say that I said, I'm going to go build this product. I'm going to clone this. I promise you, any pharmacy that I walk into, they're going to be like, you're a suit. We don't trust you. We don't like you. you know, before I even offer her or talk to them about it, they're just like, yeah, whatever, dude, not interested. She walks into pharmacies. She walks out with the customer because she said, I know you, I know your problems. I know exactly what your life is like. I'm here to help you. And they trust her, right? That distribution is such an edge. You can't replicate that, you know, that is, she's an N of one founder. There's nobody else that could do that. That's kind of what we look for. Dr. Rifkin, same thing. Nobody else could do it. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, yeah, then it goes back to, I think, where we started the conversation on the value of the founder and the people behind it. So I think that's an awesome point to leave it with you. I really appreciate. your time and all your insights before I let you go. We are ending on a segment that we call Last Call, which is a couple of hard hitting questions for you to wrap us up. So first, what is your favorite productivity tool right now? Cloud Code. All right. Good choice. You're guest on a podcast right now. All right. What speed at which do you listen to podcasts?

[SPEAKER_01]
I find it really hard to listen to podcasts and do other things because I end up getting so pulled in that I just can't do it. I'm not a big podcast listener. I just can't work and listen to podcasts. Something is going to suffer. I will tell you that my nephew graduated from college a couple years ago, and I hope his parents aren't listening. But he told me he listened to all his lectures at 3X. And I was like, that's insane. I cannot. 3. I was like, bro, are you? Yeah. I cannot. you serious right now? Like, do you actually learn anything?" And he was adamant that he retained something, but he graduated, he has a job, so we're very proud of him. That sounded crazy to me. All right. .

[SPEAKER_00]
worked for him. What's your what's your go to coffee order?

[SPEAKER_01]
So I'm actually not a big coffee drinker. I never drank coffee. Then I had kids and- And then there were just some days where I just sort of needed it. Now I drink. a decent amount of caffeine probably unhealthy amounts on my meeting days i'll stack meetings you know and like Every hour on the hour is another meeting and another cup of coffee. If I'm drinking coffee, it is just a decaf oat latte. You know, I cannot drink cup after cup of caffeine and expect to like walk in a straight line. If I'm not drinking coffee, it's usually an oat matcha. And I'm a little snobby about how they make the matcha. But my go-to here in Berkeley, there's a place that sells chai. And so I'll go there. And at first I convinced myself, like I really wanted to believe that chai had less caffeine than coffee. That is absolutely not true. But... they make a quality cup of chai.

[SPEAKER_00]
Two more quick ones for you. What's a book or TV show that you'd recommend?

[SPEAKER_01]
Okay, so I have my standard list of books, Hard Thing About Hard Things by Ben Horowitz, Chris Voss wrote Never Split the Difference. It's just a book on negotiating. It's extremely valuable. I think that the way that everyone should approach negotiations, like a lot of times what we think are negotiations really aren't, you know. And so an example that I'll use is like. founders will often walk into a meeting and say, well, my valuation, I want something between 12 and 15. Guess what answer I'm picking every single time? 12. I'm never going to like... I'm never. Like, why would I pick 15? You know, like, give me the choice, you know? And it just, it's helpful to have a better understanding of how to negotiate. What did I recently read? The Art of Gathering. I just finished that one. It was pretty interesting. How to Throw Meaningful Sort of Events. There's another one, I'm partway through 8 Million Ways to Happiness. I just randomly picked it up at the library. It's super interesting if you like Japan and Japanese culture and want a better understanding.

[SPEAKER_00]
All right, last question for you. You've been to Buffalo a bunch. We just talked to coffee shops. How about chicken wings? Drumstick or flat?

[SPEAKER_01]
I don't eat meat. Yeah. Um, You know, Buffalo actually has really good vegan food.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. It's a great foodie town.

[SPEAKER_01]
That's... Punch is well above its weight class.

[SPEAKER_00]
Awesome. Well, thank you so much for all your time.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, dude. Appreciate your time, man. We'll talk soon. I'll see you next time in town.
documents.title: Rohit Gupta, on why the Valley is looking at Buffalo

#16 Rohit Gupta - Founder & Impact Investor @ Future Communities Capital (FCC) by The Good AI Podcast
The Good AI Podcast
By Anand Sampat
In this podcast, we interview leaders at AI startups that are profitable with a purpose. These companies span any vertical and are unique in their ability to tie capital incentives to doing good in society. In these interviews we explore how they did it and post about our interviews in our newsletter at thegoodaipod.substack.com. Happy listening!
Listen on Spotify
Available on

The Good AI PodcastJan 14, 2023
Share
00:00
52:01
#19 Shabaz Patel - VP of Data Science on the potential for Good AI
How can technical leaders ensure AI is used for good? What protocols should we put in place to do that? In this episode we explore these questions and discuss how One Concern tackles these with their AI built to quantify natural disasters and build resilience.
Nov 03, 202342:16
#18 Andy Beck - CEO of PathAI on AI-Powered Pathology
PathAI builds AI-powered algorithms to extract insights from whole-slide images to faciliate drug discovery, improved clinical diagnoses and treatments of patients with cancer and other severe diseases. In this episode, we chat with Andy Beck and explore the role of AI in healthcare, biotech and the learn about how PathAI thinks about making a positive impact on the patient.
Oct 13, 202353:41
#17 Noosheen Hashemi pt. 2 - CEO & Co-founder of January AI
Noosheen is back on the pod to chat about Eden's - supplements that January AI's (https://january.ai) core virtual continuous glucose monitoring app! Chronic lifestyle diseases affect millions of Americans every year and January AI is determined to change that by changing habits and leveraging the consistency of Eden's supplements. Enjoy!
Subscribe to our newsletter for a summary of the episode: https://dwdg.substack.com.
You can find the full transcript here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/17aaJ0PTSNGEzuyAlYwW-ZGPKNFWDGB3jKMOwHFbj75M/edit.
Jun 23, 202344:17
#16 Rohit Gupta - Founder & Impact Investor @ Future Communities Capital (FCC)
In this episode we chat with Rohit Gupta, a passionate impact investor at Future Communities Capital (FCC) where he focuses on helping accelerate the growth of early stage mission-driven companies ensuring they can put fuel on the Doing Well by Doing Good fire. From introducing founders to potential customers to providing timely advice, Rohit and team help their portfolio companies sustainably Do Well while Doing Good. We chat about practical examples of his portfolio companies in healthcare and beyond and navigate the frontiers of startup land, ending with practical advice for the listeners. Enjoy!
Learn more about Rohit and his team at Future Communities Capital and their portfolio companies at https://www.futurecommunities.vc/
You can check out the portfolio companies mentioned below
- Akido Labs: https://www.akidolabs.com/
- Znest: https://znest.com/
- PlenOptika: https://plenoptika.com/
Jan 14, 202352:01
#15 Anuradha Ramachandran - Director & Investor @ Flourish Ventures
In this episode we chat with Anuradha Ramachandran, an experienced impact investor and Director at Flourish Ventures - a spinout from the Omidyar Network. She shares with us her journey investing in the financial rails for emerging markets, the ways their portfolio companies do well by doing good and her ethos for investing to balance both impact and business outcomes. Learn more about Flourish @ https://flourishventures.com/ and Anuradha @ https://www.linkedin.com/in/anuradharamachandran. Subscribe to our blog @ https://dwdg.substack.com for summaries of this and other podcasts. Enjoy!
Sep 16, 202246:15
#14 Noosheen Hashemi - CEO & Co-founder of January AI
Check out our latest episode with January AI Co-founder & CEO, Noosheen Hashemi. She is a storied Silicon Valley veteran who was critical the early growth at Oracle and has over 20 years of experience supporting nonprofits, building a family office and funding high growth businesses. In this episode we hear about how the motive to Do Well by Doing Good drove her to start January AI and how it addresses the epidemic of chronic diseases like diabetes.
We talk about her recent speech at GSB which you can find @ https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/experience/news-history/commencement/keynote-speaker-remarks
In the episode she references the concept of Ikigai - or marrying what you love, what you're good at and what the world needs. You can find more about Ikigai @ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikigai
Learn more about January AI @ https://www.january.ai/
Subscribe to our newsletter for key insights from this podcast @ https://dwdg.substack.com
Apr 05, 202254:09
#13 Brian Trelstad - HBS Professor and Partner at Bridges focused on Service-Based Impact Investment
Brian Trelstad teaches Social Entrepreneurship and Social Change at Harvard Business School and is a long-time impact investor. Brian is currently a Partner of the US Sustainability Growth Fund at Bridges investing in service-based companies making a difference. In this episode, he shares his experiences at Acumen, the thesis of his current fund Bridges US Sustainability Growth Fund, and provides examples of portfolio companies Doing Well by Doing Good via the for-profit services they provide.
Learn more about Brian and his work at Bridges US Sustainability Growth Fund: https://www.bridgesfundmanagement.com/us/team/brian-trelstad/
Learn more about Brian and his teaching at HBS: https://www.hbs.edu/faculty/Pages/profile.aspx?facId=1132519
Nov 22, 202134:37
#12 Vikram Gandhi - HBS Professor and Managing Partner at Asha Impact Fund
Vikram Gandhi is a Professor of Sustainable Investing at Harvard Business School, a long-time investor, and the Managing Partner at Asha Impact Fund, an India-focused fund investing in product and services companies across multiple sectors. In this episode Vikram talks about his journey and the impetus for starting Asha Impact. We also explore the portfolio companies that are Doing Well by Doing Good and explore how impact investing is like traditional financing and what makes it different.
Learn more about Vikram's teaching: https://www.hbs.edu/faculty/Pages/profile.aspx?facId=103852
Learn more about Asha Impact Fund: https://ashaimpact.com/
Oct 04, 202145:04
#11 CEO of MyFugo Allan Tollo on Funding Rural Farmers in Kenya
CEO of Kenya-based Smart Agriculture company MyFugo, Allan Tollo, talks about his experience witnessing the struggle of rural farmers in Kenya finding a way build a sustainable livelihood and how he leveraged his technical background to engineer a data-driven solution. Allan walks us through the business model -- Doing Well -- and tangible examples of the positive impact MyFugo is already having with its customers -- Doing Good.
You can learn more about MyFugo at http://myfugo.com/
Sep 05, 202143:17
#10 Elevar Equity Partner Sandeep Farias on DWDG Portfolio Companies
In Part 2 of our conversation with Sandeep Farias, we go deeper into how the Elevar Method is used in practice with a few examples and talk about how they Do Well by Doing Good using the LAHWS framework. Listen in to hear about Elevar's investments and for some advice for the listeners on how to think about making an impact by joining or creating your own DWDG startup.
Jun 20, 202135:02
#9 Elevar Equity Partner Sandeep Farias on Measuring Good & the COVID Crisis in India
Elevar Equity is an early stage impact fund focused on funding companies that tackle fundamental problems for low income populations in LatAm and India. We sat down with Sandeep Farias where he describes The Elevar Method of investing in companies that follow the Low ARPU, High Wallet Share (aka LAHWS) framework and talk deeply about the recent COVID crisis in India and how DWDG companies can help. Listen in for Part 1 of this episode and stay tuned for Part 2 where we delve deeper into examples of DWDG portfolio companies and advice for the listeners.
Jun 13, 202137:02
#8 Leaf Global CEO Nat Robinson on Financial Services for Refugees
Nat Robinson, CEO of Leaf Global, and author of the book Creating a Cash Cow in Kenya, talks to us about building social enterprises, raising money from investors, and the motivation for building financial services for the unbanked and highly vulnerable refugee population. Listen in to hear his stories of building businesses in Africa and his advice for the next social enterprise entrepreneur. Learn more about Leaf and their work here @ https://leafglobalfintech.com/ and check out Nat's book at https://www.amazon.com/dp/B01AOB7BWE/
Mar 04, 202137:36
#7 Perlara CEO Ethan Perlstein on New Models in Biopharma
CEO, cure sherpa, and entrepreneur-scientist Ethan Perlstein joins us to talk about how Biopharma PBC Perlara works with families, patient organizations, and researchers to develop cures for rare diseases. In this podcast, we learn how it all got started, how Perlara is taking a novel approach to the traditional Pharma business model to create recurring revenue models which Do Well by Doing Good, and end with some advice for listeners looking to follow a similar approach. Learn more @ https://www.perlara.com/ or Tweet Ethan @eperlste
Feb 09, 202123:40
#6 One Concern CEO Ahmad Wani on Building a Resilient World
In this episode we chat with Ahmad Wani, the CEO of One Concern about Doing Well by Doing Good in the sustainability and climate change space. We discuss mission, culture, and the intersection of Doing Well and profitability with Social Good. You can find out more about One Concern and careers on their Website: https://oneconcern.com and recent work on their Medium page: https://medium.com/@oneconcerninc.
Dec 04, 202031:60
#5 Bonus: What we've learned so far in < 5 min
In this episode, we explore the key takeaways from our interviews in less than 5 min. We explore questions like what does it take to found a company? how can we create sustainable companies? how does culture play a role? how can one make the leap? But we'd love to hear from you too! What do you think? Are there any insights we missed? Tweet us @dwdgsf or email us at hello@doingwellbydoinggood.co.
Oct 30, 202004:41
#4 Copia CEO Komal Ahmad on Solving Hunger - "The World's Dumbest Problem"
Copia CEO Komal Ahmad joins us to talk about how her Public Benefit Corporation is solving hunger in the US today and eventually throughout the globe. We talk mission, culture, Doing Well by Doing Good, and how a PBC differs from a traditional C-corp but still enforces a high-growth mindset, with a legally-binding social bend.
Oct 07, 202040:15
#3 Shelf Engine CEO Stefan Kalb on Solving Food Waste, One Item At a Time
Shelf Engine Co-founder & CEO Stefan Kalb joins us to talk about fixing the food waste problem and building a sustainable Doing Well by Doing Good business in the process. Shelf Engine is a Seattle-based started, which recently raised a seed round and is growing. To learn more about how it works check out this video.
Aug 26, 202027:18
#2 Ride Health CEO Imran Cronk on Better Healthcare through Better Transit
Ride Health Co-founder and CEO Imran Cronk joins us to talk about how Ride Health is positioning itself to change the world, and how they are building a sustainable, high-growth Doing Well by Doing Good business in the process. Ride Health is a seed stage startup ensuring transit is never a barrier to healthcare access. You can find the original Atlantic article written by Imran and referenced in the episode here.
Aug 20, 202029:48
#1 Nova Credit CEO Misha Esipov on Financial Freedom for Immigrants
Nova Credit Co-founder and CEO Misha Esipov joins us to talk about their approach to building a for-profit, VC-backed, high-growth social enterprise and how they approach Doing Well by Doing Good in their business and culture. Nova Credit recently raised a Series B, and is growing. For a quick overview of Nova Credit's business check out this CNBC interview.

Check out the trailer introducing the podcast. In this we cover a quick overview of what we mean by Doing Well by Doing Good, who we plan to highlight, why we created this, and how we plan to achieve the goal. #169 Mappa: Can Voice AI Find You a Job… or a Date?
The Pitch
Oct 8, 202553 minInvestor
AI Summary
→ WHAT IT COVERS
Sarah Luzena pitches MAPPA, a voice analysis AI company achieving $3.5M ARR in two years that decodes behavioral traits through speech patterns to improve hiring, dating, and interpersonal connections beyond traditional resumes.
→ KEY INSIGHTS
- **Voice signal extraction:** MAPPA analyzes linguistic markers like first-person pronouns and verb density plus prosodic signals including pitch, jitter, shimmer, and pauses to create behavioral profiles without personality boxes, training models on academic studies and customer feedback loops.
- **Success-based pricing model:** Companies pay 25% of monthly salary for every hire made through MAPPA for the entire employment duration, achieving 92% interview-to-hire conversion rates and reducing hiring timelines from three months to under one week with 78% repeat customer rates.
- **Horizontal expansion strategy:** Beyond recruiting, MAPPA launched API access at $12 per report serving seven universities tracking student development, venture capital firms vetting founders, and dating apps enhancing matching algorithms while maintaining 94% SaaS margins versus 82% on recruiting.
- **Cultural accent adaptation:** The system trains separate models by geographic region to handle prosodic differences like volume variations across cultures, scraping LinkedIn profiles and metadata to automatically apply the correct behavioral analysis framework and avoid bias from regional speech patterns.
→ NOTABLE MOMENT
The founder revealed she closed the seed round at $15M valuation two months prior, then proposed a $48M extension valuation to investors, tripling her company worth despite warnings this aggressive jump would scare off most potential backers.

#171 Doctours: VC Funded Hair Transplants?!
The Pitch
Oct 22, 202542 minInvestor, Future Communities Capital
AI Summary
→ WHAT IT COVERS
Doctours founder Gheeram pitches a medical tourism marketplace starting with Turkish hair transplants, raising $1M at $8M valuation with $850K committed, generating $20K revenue from 50 bookings via TikTok marketing.
→ KEY INSIGHTS
- **Marketplace unit economics:** Doctours charges tiered commissions of 10% for first 10 patients per clinic monthly, 20% for patients 11-20, and 30% beyond 20 patients, currently averaging 10% take rate on $200K GMV.
- **Customer acquisition arbitrage:** The company acquires users for $200 through TikTok micro-influencers while earning $500-$1500 per booking, achieving profitability on first transaction before adding recurring revenue through medication partnerships like finasteride prescriptions.
- **Clinic verification process:** Three-person Turkey team physically visits 415 Istanbul clinics, validates local and international certifications with government offices, and rejects over 50% of applicants who use borrowed, expired, or fraudulent credentials before platform listing.
- **Vertical expansion criteria:** Select markets where Americans already travel abroad, price differences exceed 10x versus US costs, and total addressable market reaches billions—IVF at $25B annually qualifies, requiring 45-day Spain stays at $5K versus US prices.
→ NOTABLE MOMENT
When Gheeram revealed his life-saving medical tourism story about his brother's heart condition, then pivoted to building the business around elective hair transplants, investors struggled to reconcile the mission-driven narrative with the cosmetic surgery reality.

#175 Above Health: The Allergy Clinic of the Future
The Pitch
Nov 19, 202547 minInvestor
AI Summary
→ WHAT IT COVERS
Matt Truby pitches Above Health, an AI diagnostic platform combining telehealth, custom lab panels, and proprietary hardware devices to revolutionize allergy and asthma care, raising $450,000 from four investors at a $10 million valuation.
→ KEY INSIGHTS
- **Hardware cost innovation:** Matt builds clinical-grade devices at unprecedented prices—a smart inhaler with GPS for $1,000 per prototype iteration and a diagnostic stethoscope for $9.99 manufacturing cost, compared to traditional costs of $500,000 and $88 respectively, enabling mass distribution.
- **Value-based care acceleration:** Above Health targets value-based care contracts within two years instead of the typical five by combining telehealth with proprietary devices as differentiators, starting with underserved markets like Kern County with 700,000 people and zero allergists.
- **Precision diagnostics approach:** The platform uses GPS-enabled inhalers to capture location, pollen, and air quality data within one square kilometer, then offers targeted lab testing for specific allergens like Cottonwood instead of expensive 50-allergen panels with 20% false positives.
- **Market entry strategy:** Customer acquisition cost of $10 through free at-home allergy stickers promoted on parent forums, booking telehealth visits through October while building toward retail distribution and health system contracts, maintaining $3,000-4,000 monthly burn rate with just the founder full-time.
→ NOTABLE MOMENT
Matt's daughter experienced anaphylaxis from yogurt, triggering AI alerts from her Apple Watch detecting elevated heart rate, cough patterns, and dropping oxygen levels—the personal crisis that drove him to dedicate his career to building comprehensive allergy care solutions.

TIEN WONG, CEO, OPUS8, INC.
Tien is Founder and Host of the Big Idea CONNECTpreneur Community, a global community

E1: Rohit Gupta, on why the Valley is looking at Buffalo
Interviewing the builders, doers, and creators powering Buffalo's economic revival.
‍
Rohit Gupta is Managing Director at Future Communities Capital, a fund backing founders transforming legacy industries. His investments span companies like SpaceX and Lyft, and in Buffalo include HELIX Intel and Ognomy.
‍
In this episode, Rohit breaks down why he’s betting on places outside Silicon Valley and what he sees in Buffalo specifically. We talk about how he first got connected to the region, what keeps bringing him back, and why some of the best opportunities are hiding in overlooked markets.
‍
We also get into what founders still get wrong when raising capital, how much networks actually matter, and his view on building companies in the age of AI.

Future Frontier Capital
How We Got Here
In 1992, my father, Irving Rappaport co-founded Smart Patents, one 
of the ﬁrst companies to convert the world’s paper patent repository 
into digital format. They initially developed tools for synchronizing, 
displaying, and manipulating text and image documents on a digital 
display. This technology enabled people to compare, highlight, and 
analyze two patents side by side on a screen. This was revolutionary, 
as attorneys used to do everything on paper. Later, the company 
changed its name to Aurigin Systems and became a big data pioneer.
Once the world’s patent information was online, they realized it could 
be used for business, R&D and IP decision making. Patent analytics 
and patent landscape analysis, two ﬁelds Aurigin pioneered, enable 
the use of patent information to gain a more complete picture of a 
competitive landscape. Patent landscapes and analytics help us 
understand technology development trends, track companies’ R&D, 
gain insight into where companies intend to sell or manufacture 
products by looking at geographic patent ﬁlings, and even provide 
insights into how to build the next disruptive technology. One of the 
crown jewels of Aurigin’s technology stack was a patent mapping & 
visualization tool that generated topographic maps called 
Themescape. My colleague T ony Trippe, who worked at Aurigin, 
provides an excellent overview of Themescape and other spatial 
patent mapping technologies on his Patinformatics blog.
Future Frontier Capital www.futurefrontier.vc matt@futurefrontier.vc
How is Future Frontier 
Capital (FFC) different 
from other early stage 
venture capital ﬁrms?
FFC stands apart from other VC funds in several ways. We have a 
unique processes for ﬁnding outstanding opportunities in technology 
landscapes, and helping portfolio companies grow. 
One differentiator is our proprietary software to screen companies, 
and quickly identify trends and opportunities in emerging technology 
categories. 
A second differentiator is our ability to mentor companies on 
technical challenges, and connect startups with the right advisors 
with technical, licensing, or IP experience. 
Finally, through our experience running an IP strategy and analytics 
ﬁrm, we have an outstanding network of patent attorneys, technical 
experts, government lab/university contacts, and corporate 
innovation groups. This network provides us very early access to 
startups resulting in unique and exceptional deal ﬂow. 
A little bit of history on 
how we got here.

The technology was one of the early examples that combined self- 
organizing map algorithms with term frequency inverted document 
frequency algorithms. The output placed each patent on a three 
dimensional map. Here is an example of what those maps looked like:
Future Frontier Capital www.futurefrontier.vc rohit@futurefrontier.vc
At the time, these were 
powerful representations to 
help patent and non-patent 
experts understand the 
relationships between 
companies’ patents through 
a visual tool. CEOs and 
investors used these maps to 
understand the competitive 
patent landscape. However, 
there was a misconception 
that these maps were 
powerful enough to rely on 
for making business 
decisions.
Although useful, these maps are only scratching the surface to 
understand competitive activity in the patent landscape. Additional 
analysis is required, including reading the patents, and generating 
more in-depth analytics. That said, versions of this technology are 
still used today to understand relationships between technology, 
patents, and competitors in a technology category. Some tech-focused, 
large corporations use patent analytics to support fundamental 
business decisions such as, should we build or buy new technology? 
For startups, patent analytics help understand issues such such as:
1. Are there other technologies that provide better, faster or cheaper 
solutions to the problem we are trying to solve? 
How should we deal with these?
2. Where are the gaps in large company portfolios that we might ﬁll?
3. What companies (patents) might we come up against if we launch a 
successful product in an industry?
Future Frontier Capital
How We Got Here


Future Frontier Capital www.futurefrontier.vc rohit@futurefrontier.vc
Before launching IP Checkups, the patent analytics and strategy 
ﬁrm I co-founded in 2004, I interned as a public equity analyst for 
one of my mentors, John McCamant at the Medical T echnology 
Stock Letter.  At the time, I was one of the only people using patent 
analytics to identify companies with rich and defensible IP , and see 
if that correlated with stock price outperformance compared to 
individual competitors and stock market indices. 
I quickly learned that it was difficult to ﬁnd an edge when 
comparing large companies. However, for smaller companies and 
microcaps, I was able to signiﬁcantly outperform the market and the 
Russell 2000 index.
The success motivated me to move forward, and I spent hours 
digging into different technology categories (patent landscapes) to 
understand who the players were, and how they were positioned 
from an IP perspective. Simultaneously, I launched IP Checkups (IPC) 
to offer consulting services to large companies on how to use patent 
analytics to make informed business and technology development 
decisions.
In 2005, IPC partnered with IBM’s Almaden Research Lab  to 
collaborate on the development of next generation patent and text 
analytics tools. In order to run the necessary software and 
hardware, I needed to hire help,. Around this time, a mutual friend 
introduced me to Mark Garner Casaña. 
Mark and I met for coffee and connected over our shared interest in 
music. I had worked as a professional musician early in my career and 
Mark was working as a sound technician with major musical touring 
acts across the US and Europe. Although he enjoyed the music 
industry, he studied computer science in college and was looking to 
try something new.. Over several conversations he decided to join 
me and help build out our patent analytics platform
Mark led IPC’s initiative starting in 2007 to build our own software 
to manage competitive patents and technical literature, which made 
comparing competitor portfolios efficient and easy to keep current. 
I continued to ﬁnd alpha from analyzing portfolios of small publicly 
traded companies, but as our consulting services and software 
business grew, I focused on IPC. 
Our proprietary 
software screens 
companies and quickly 
identiﬁes trends and 
opportunities.
Future Frontier Capital
How We Got Here


Future Frontier Capital www.futurefrontier.vc rohit@futurefrontier.vc
Between 2007 and 2022 we performed hundreds of technology 
landscape analysis and strategy consulting projects. We analyzed 
dozens of frontier technology areas for companies of all sizes. These 
engagements made us experts in using patent information to make 
informed business, R&D, and IP decisions. Along the way, Mark 
continued to build our our software and analytics capabilities. 
Coming full circle, we started investing in early stage startups. We 
provided our services and software in exchange for equity, helping 
our clients build durable and defensible innovation programs. This 
led to an engagement with a small startup in 2017 that grew very 
rapidly and led to a public market IPO exit in 2019. After building a 
strong portfolio of individual investments, the natural next step was 
to launch a VC fund. 
In early 2021, I was introduced to Rohit Gupta, a Berkeley based 
Venture Capitalist. Rohit began his career in real-estate, working 
with his family to invest in real estate in the Bay Area and beyond. 
In 2008, during the great recession, Rohit was inspired to branch 
out. He began making Venture Capital investments out of his family 
office. 
Several of his early investments were big winners, yet his family was 
uninterested in diversifying their investments. Rohit went out alone 
as a solo General Partner and raised two funds under the name 
Future Communities Capital (FCC). 
When Rohit and I met, he was fascinated by our unique approach to 
spotting and mentoring early-stage startups. He was also impressed 
by our early deal-ﬂow and the quality of our founders and startups. 
He suggested that Mark and I join FCC and we raise a new preseed 
fund focused on writing the ﬁrst check to frontier technology 
companies.
In early 2023, Rohit (Managing Partner), Mark Garner Casaña 
(CTO/Data Scientist), and I announced our new fund, Future 
Frontier Capital. We apply many of the lessons, tools, and methods 
developed at IPC and FCC to identify and invest in interesting 
startups working in emerging technology categories.
FFC applys our 
experience in IP 
analytics and strategy 
with VC investing to 
identify and invest in 
exceptional startups
Future Frontier Capital

Our Team
Rohit Gupta — Managing Director
Rohit Gupta is the Managing Director of Future Communities Capital (FCC). Rohit has led investments into Coupang, Counsyl, Biomeme, SpaceX, Akido, Lyft, Roofr, and more.
FCC looks for technology entrepreneurs focused on disrupting legacy industries such as government, healthcare, finance, and real estate. Portfolio companies are tackling problems ranging from smart city infrastructure to disease outbreak management.
Rohit holds an MS in Environmental Engineering from Cornell University. He completed his BS at the University of Southern California.
Advisors
Neil Daswani Co-Director at the Stanford Advanced Security Certification Program
Neil Daswani is Co-Director of the Stanford Advanced Security Certification Program, and has also served as an Executive-in Residence at Trinity Ventures. He has in the past served in a variety of research, development, teaching, and executive roles at Symantec, LifeLock, Twitter, Dasient, Google, NTT DoCoMo USA Labs, Yodlee, and Bellcore. Neil has been both a security entrepreneur having co-founded Dasient which was acquired by Twitter, and has also served as a Chief Information Security Officer at LifeLock and at Symantec's Consumer Business Unit. His DNA is deeply rooted in security research and development, he has dozens of technical articles published in top academic and industry conferences (ACM, IEEE, USENIX, RSA, BlackHat, and OWASP), and he has been granted over a dozen U.S. patents. Neil is also co-author of "Foundations of Security: What Every Programmer Needs To Know." He earned Ph.D. and M.S. degrees in Computer Science at Stanford University, and he holds a B.S. in Computer Science with honors with distinction from Columbia University.
Sanjit Mahanti Head of Business Development at Akido Labs
Sanjit has over 15 years of technology and innovation experience in the healthcare space. His dynamic and evolving expertise includes executive leadership positions in academic healthcare, population management and technology. During his tenure as Chief Business Development Officer for Keck Medicine of USC, he was instrumental in the creation of the organization’s innovation management function. Sanjit holds a Bachelor of Arts in Economics from University of Michigan and a Master’s in Health Administration from University of Southern California Price School. He lectures regularly on the business and technology transformations of American healthcare and currently sits on the Board of Adventist Health Glendale.
Andrew PoksayClimate Fellow at FCI
Andrew Poksay has nearly a decade of experience disrupting legacy industries and building companies that create meaningful impact. He is currently a member of the executive team at Akido Labs, where he has led product and ops teams, helping to scale the company from five people in a garage to over 500 people across the world.
Andrew is an active member of the climate change community. In addition to investing in and advising startups tackling climate change problems, he supports climate activism organizations from his hometown of Seattle.
Brad SelbyChief Administrative Officer for the Department of Surgery and the Executive Administrator of the USC Cardiac and Vascular Institute at the University of Southern California
Brad Selby is a healthcare executive with 33 years of experience working in academic medical centers. Mr. Selby is a member of the Board of Directors of Wescom Credit Union, a $6 billion credit union based in Pasadena, CA. He also serves on the Board of Directors of Wound Care Advantage, a national wound care company with 44 locations across the United States, and he advises healthcare startups. Mr. Selby received a BA in Biology from the University of Missouri-Columbia and an MBA from Colorado State University.

About
Future Communities Capital is a Berkeley, California-based early-stage venture capital firm that provides pre-seed and seed funding to technology entrepreneurs disrupting legacy industries. The investment vehicle focuses on backing mission-driven companies building innovative solutions to address complex global challenges, ranging from smart city infrastructure development to infectious disease outbreak management. Beyond supplying initial financial backing, the organization actively assists its portfolio companies by leveraging its network to facilitate high-value customer introductions that accelerate commercial growth. The firm targets traditional sectors requiring modernization, specifically allocating capital toward startups operating within healthcare, government, finance, real estate, property technology, energy, and supply chain logistics. The organization's historical investment portfolio features several recognizable technology enterprises and successful ventures, including SpaceX, Lyft, Coupang, Biomeme, and Counsyl. Future Communities Capital was established by its founder and managing director, Rohit Gupta.

🎙️ Rohit Gupta - Founder and Impact Investor @ Future Communities Capital 💵 — Anand Sampat
Anand Sampat
🎙️ Rohit Gupta - Founder and Impact Investor @ Future Communities Capital 💵
January 17, 2023
original link: https://thegoodaipod.substack.com/p/rohit-gupta-founder-and-impact-investor
Impact Investing for a Better World focused on Healthtech and Fintech
Jan 17, 2023
Happy New Year! 🎉 2022 has been an exciting one! Markets have had their ups and downs and 2023 looks like it’s going to be as wild a ride. Thankfully, the goodness of humanity is a beacon of light and the number of companies Doing Well by Doing Good continues to increase 🚀!
In 2023 we’re re-committing to chat with as many founders and investors to learn how they do it and to inspire others to do the same. 2022 saw much of the market and the technology industry drop but many companies committed to strong missions, showing strong growth and sober valuations survive. Much like the 2008 crash, many of the best companies thrived by embracing frugality and focus and went on to become behemoths — Dropbox, Airbnb and many others!
In this episode recorded in March 2022 we chatted with Rohit Gupta , founder and impact investor at Future Communities Capital (FCC) focused on mission-driven companies across all industries with a slight bend toward healthcare because of how the fund started and Rohit’s own background in the biotech space. As always, if you’re interested in the whole episode peruse the Spotify preview below, or cruise over to the bullet points below for specific points of the conversation and the TLDR; Enjoy!
Background and Journey
[1:15] What was your journey and how did you get into impact investing?
Worked in genetic labs in undergrad and met the Counsyl (acq. by Myriad Genetics in 2018) team 14 years ago which lead to the first investment.
Future Communities Capital came out of this desire to invest in healthtech, biotech and finding opportunities for large-scale change (e.g. Counsyl’s vision was to eliminate inherited diseases)
Unique differentiator - focused on mission-driven companies primarily but not exclusively in healthcare and committed to delivering value via high-value intros to accelerate sales (e.g. a novel healthtech looking to sell to health systems)
Portfolio Companies - Growth and Mission
[ 8:45[] How do your portfolio companies sustain growth and evolve business models? ](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=gEjh0jK4SQmPbyE4qAN_BA&t=525&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R)
Example : Akido Labs started as a platform to make ineffectual unstructured healthcare data valuable. FCC introduced them to customers to accelerate growth. They doubled down on their vulnerable patient population and decided to become a complete care delivery platform for that vertical.
[ 13:01[] How do you ensure multiple stakeholders are on the same page as the company](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=23nLYXs2QHSMSbtpmCVaKg&t=780&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R) grows and shifts directions to maintain the mission?
Growth and making money solves all problems, but a strong mission-driven company culture that perpetuates through growth can ensure stakeholders are on board throughout.
[ 15:40[] How do you determine stickiness of the product or service of a potential portfolio company and how assess the metrics at the early stage?](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=q2uGdQhuRPqvZ1mJtQJTkw&t=939&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R)
Key is to identify that the founder knows the industry they are selling to, have built trusted relationships with customers and are able and willing to roll up their sleeves and get their hands dirty.
Example : Znest facilitates finding the right senior community living by making pricing more transparent. The founder is an expert in real estate and can call on REIT owners to put their senior housing facilities on the platform.
Measuring Doing Well and Doing Good
[ 19:45[] How do you measure doing well and doing good? ](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=vaSlvVqcRA2dHoRsdK4xVg&t=1185&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R)
Prior to Series B / A, the metrics are often off anyways so it’s best to look at the model rather than the absolute numbers.
Goal setting and plan-making is more important than the absolute numbers at the early stage.
[ 21:50[] Conflicts between Doing Well and Doing Good ](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=e08oIAw-QrqAUjaDy6h5MQ&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R&t=1308)
Public companies have a much harder time than private companies because public markets provide more scrutiny than private companies
Private companies face challenges only when the board doesn’t see eye-to-eye with the founders. Board formation is critical at the early stage for that reason.
Building trust with vulnerable customers is hard to build and conflicts with the mission could hamper that. It’s important to not undermine it
E.g. 70 million jobs - training and finding employment for formerly incarcerated people. the founder Richard is focused on maintaining trust with that community
Sustaining Doing Good as Companies Grow
[ 28:55[] How do companies sustain Doing Good as they grow (esp. after becoming public)? ](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=AF3GPQtjQH21dlBNcdbq_g&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R&t=1735)
Healthcare companie s have an easier time as long as they are focused on patients but for housing or fintech companies it’s much harder
B-corp, ESG and non-profit arms are some ways public companies are already committing to Doing Good but hard to point to many public companies doing incrementally more good for every unit of additional revenue earned.
Private companies and public companies have to balance demands of customers, stakeholders and the broader market (including potential future customers).
[ 37:25[] How are portfolio companies thinking about this?](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=UuV8DSV-SdqjNBAlkZqyOA&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R&t=2243)
PlenOptika — affordable and portable optometry care for vulnerable populations. Early care gets them 90% to where they need to be and preventative for downstream diseases — e.g. early onset dementia
Akido Labs — healthcare for vulnerable populations is a critical but only providing services isn’t enough — building clinics to serve these populations closes the clinical loop and better solves the root issues.
Advice for Listeners
[ 40:45[] Advice for to-be DWDG founders ](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=gboDbhRGS8-AbAdEsJZGsA&t=2445&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R)
Be mission driven — make sure the company is something you care about deeply. Ideally if the company’s mission is your life’s work and you could not imagine doing anything else it will be hard for you to fail
Be a great person — Being a good person enables you to afford opportunities that you wouldn’t have otherwise. Surround yourself with good people and emulate that, you are who you surround yourself with
[ 44:00[] Advice for DWDG professionals ](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=u3MuuIjcQj2-vY2oQ9uxhw&t=2640&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R)
Don’t burn yourself out — you are your hardest critic. Use a reliable technique, meditation, gratitude or reflection journals or other calming techniques
_ Extend your network_ — often by the time you realize you need a network is much later than you really needed it.
[ 47:55[] Advice for “people in power” (e.g. VCs, successful founders, influencers, etc.)](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1tu6ESK9pC7Wo0naAj1YMn?si=CQ9MRzxeT1Cx8dEN2FyKoA&context=spotify%3Ashow%3A4ZpKwhV1xihtsJzcOeKu9R&t=2875)
_ Open up your network_ — When you have a network connect people to help those who could benefit from it. It can never hurt and is always a win-win
Thanks for listening and tuning in to the latest episode and our first for 2023! Wishing you an amazing new year full of Doing Well and Doing Good! Until the next time just remember as you start the new year that…
If you liked what you read or heard please share with your friends and family!
Thank you for reading Doing Well By Doing Good. This post is public so feel free to share it.
Share
And of course if you need the podcast link again check it out here. Upwards and onwards 🚀!
✌🏽Anand

documents.text:
🎙️ Rohit Gupta - Founder and Impact Investor @ Future Communities Capital 💵
The Good AI Podcast
SubscribeSign in
🎙️ Rohit Gupta - Founder and Impact Investor @ Future Communities Capital 💵
Impact Investing for a Better World focused on Healthtech and Fintech
Anand Sampat
Jan 17, 2023
Share
Happy New Year! 🎉 2022 has been an exciting one! Markets have had their ups and downs and 2023 looks like it’s going to be as wild a ride. Thankfully, the goodness of humanity is a beacon of light and the number of companies Doing Well by Doing Good continues to increase 🚀!
In 2023 we’re re-committing to chat with as many founders and investors to learn how they do it and to inspire others to do the same. 2022 saw much of the market and the technology industry drop but many companies committed to strong missions, showing strong growth and sober valuations survive. Much like the 2008 crash, many of the best companies thrived by embracing frugality and focus and went on to become behemoths — Dropbox, Airbnb and many others!
Thanks for reading Doing Well By Doing Good! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support this work.
Subscribe
In this episode recorded in March 2022 we chatted with Rohit Gupta, founder and impact investor at Future Communities Capital (FCC) focused on mission-driven companies across all industries with a slight bend toward healthcare because of how the fund started and Rohit’s own background in the biotech space. As always, if you’re interested in the whole episode peruse the Spotify preview below, or cruise over to the bullet points below for specific points of the conversation and the TLDR; Enjoy!
Background and Journey
[1:15] What was your journey and how did you get into impact investing?
Worked in genetic labs in undergrad and met the Counsyl (acq. by Myriad Genetics in 2018) team 14 years ago which lead to the first investment.
Future Communities Capital came out of this desire to invest in healthtech, biotech and finding opportunities for large-scale change (e.g. Counsyl’s vision was to eliminate inherited diseases)
Unique differentiator - focused on mission-driven companies primarily but not exclusively in healthcare and committed to delivering value via high-value intros to accelerate sales (e.g. a novel healthtech looking to sell to health systems)
Portfolio Companies - Growth and Mission
[8:45] How do your portfolio companies sustain growth and evolve business models?
Example: Akido Labs started as a platform to make ineffectual unstructured healthcare data valuable. FCC introduced them to customers to accelerate growth. They doubled down on their vulnerable patient population and decided to become a complete care delivery platform for that vertical.
[13:01] How do you ensure multiple stakeholders are on the same page as the company grows and shifts directions to maintain the mission?
Growth and making money solves all problems, but a strong mission-driven company culture that perpetuates through growth can ensure stakeholders are on board throughout.
[15:40] How do you determine stickiness of the product or service of a potential portfolio company and how assess the metrics at the early stage?
Key is to identify that the founder knows the industry they are selling to, have built trusted relationships with customers and are able and willing to roll up their sleeves and get their hands dirty.
Example: Znest facilitates finding the right senior community living by making pricing more transparent. The founder is an expert in real estate and can call on REIT owners to put their senior housing facilities on the platform.
Measuring Doing Well and Doing Good
[19:45] How do you measure doing well and doing good?
Prior to Series B / A, the metrics are often off anyways so it’s best to look at the model rather than the absolute numbers.
Goal setting and plan-making is more important than the absolute numbers at the early stage.
[21:50] Conflicts between Doing Well and Doing Good
Public companies have a much harder time than private companies because public markets provide more scrutiny than private companies
Private companies face challenges only when the board doesn’t see eye-to-eye with the founders. Board formation is critical at the early stage for that reason.
Building trust with vulnerable customers is hard to build and conflicts with the mission could hamper that. It’s important to not undermine it
E.g. 70 million jobs - training and finding employment for formerly incarcerated people. the founder Richard is focused on maintaining trust with that community
Sustaining Doing Good as Companies Grow
[28:55] How do companies sustain Doing Good as they grow (esp. after becoming public)?
Healthcare companies have an easier time as long as they are focused on patients but for housing or fintech companies it’s much harder
B-corp, ESG and non-profit arms are some ways public companies are already committing to Doing Good but hard to point to many public companies doing incrementally more good for every unit of additional revenue earned.
Private companies and public companies have to balance demands of customers, stakeholders and the broader market (including potential future customers).
[37:25] How are portfolio companies thinking about this?
PlenOptika — affordable and portable optometry care for vulnerable populations. Early care gets them 90% to where they need to be and preventative for downstream diseases — e.g. early onset dementia
Akido Labs — healthcare for vulnerable populations is a critical but only providing services isn’t enough — building clinics to serve these populations closes the clinical loop and better solves the root issues.
Advice for Listeners
[40:45] Advice for to-be DWDG founders
Be mission driven — make sure the company is something you care about deeply. Ideally if the company’s mission is your life’s work and you could not imagine doing anything else it will be hard for you to fail
Be a great person — Being a good person enables you to afford opportunities that you wouldn’t have otherwise. Surround yourself with good people and emulate that, you are who you surround yourself with
[44:00] Advice for DWDG professionals
Don’t burn yourself out — you are your hardest critic. Use a reliable technique, meditation, gratitude or reflection journals or other calming techniques
Extend your network — often by the time you realize you need a network is much later than you really needed it.
[47:55] Advice for “people in power” (e.g. VCs, successful founders, influencers, etc.)
Open up your network — When you have a network connect people to help those who could benefit from it. It can never hurt and is always a win-win
Thanks for listening and tuning in to the latest episode and our first for 2023! Wishing you an amazing new year full of Doing Well and Doing Good! Until the next time just remember as you start the new year that…
If you liked what you read or heard please share with your friends and family!
